title: 100% procedural mech generation. There are no pre-baked 3d models used here, it's all math and generated on the fly. These are then boned, jointed, and rigged and exported for UE5 for control in game. 150 parts per mech, 150k tri on average.
author: codeninja

comments.author: BrandenBegins

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
No one prompt. Lots and lots and lots of iterative design. Start with a function that distributes connection points evenly across the surface which a leg or appendage would attach to. Then move from there to sculpt the skeleton, then work from there to design modular parts. 

Iterate until spider.

replies.author: sans5z
replies.body: What would I need to do if I want to do something similar? Is there any content you'd suggest to learn?

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Have Claude walk you though Procedural design, procedural metallic textures, mesh generation and deformation, and build a layered modular skeletal system with rigged joints with range controls and ever so slightly elastic controls. Layer armor grime, scratches, hammered, and decals and damage in the textures. 

I have Claude code and codex both connected to the blender and UE MCP server. 

All of the spider parts are code, each foot is code, then the lower leg, then that ankle attachment, then then foot wiggle, then the knee... and then iterate...

replies.author: sans5z
replies.body: Thanks

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Take it slow and before you begin, get a good picture in your head of what your end goal will be and then really articulate that well so that you set the vision. 

Outline the vision, and then have claude research the hell out of that and find source material. Build up your wiki of context. Find research papers and state of the art git repo demos. You'll pull a lot of good resource from that. 

Spiders are not my vision, Procedural generation is my vision. Spiders were just the most complex thing I could think of to try first.

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Yes.

Use math. Start with a cylindrical tube. Make a point. Glue it to another tube with a joint. make that work. Iterate and repeat. Then when I had a tube spider, I started iterating on the parts, 125 parts per spider with gears and joints. Small parts compile into bigger parts with algos... 

This function returns a hash of gear configs, this function aligns all the parts I pass it in horizontal 3d space with center alignment. this function makes them all touch, this function wires them to turn in sequence to the relative motion of the leg... that's your knee. 

Then you have a leggie... and little pincers... and all the do dads. and all that attaches to joint points you can distribute so you can have 2, 4,6, 8, 100 legs... and body segments, and spines, and tails, and whips and wings....

comments.body: Did the ai write the algorithm or is it generating every thing using tokens over and over?

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Every part has a function in the code that codes the geometry for that part. Parts get layered on top of other parts that makes a thorax. The thorax gets bolted onto joints and the joints get bolted onto legs.

There's a function for distributing joints evenly around the body. There's another function for making joints, articulate in certain positions and angles based on the position on the body. 

All the movement is procedurally generated in real time and calculated by the engine as you move, so there's no prebaked animations, it's all just math.

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Make a box with code, give it joints and legs. Wonder how many legs is too many legs... achieve spider.

Every spider is procedurally generated with math joint by joint. All the 3d objects that make up the spider's body are just mathematical formulas that generate polygons in blender.

No hard coded models.

I wanted to see how far I could get with math alone. And you can get pretty far.

I will make a detailed post later that goes into a lot more depth
